title: Conventions: what a chain is, and how to write one
body:
## Note

### Notation

Inverses are written as upper case letters: `A` means the inverse of `a`. Do not write
`a^{-1}`, `a\inv`, or anything else. Formal chains are written as sums, with `+`.

So `a + bABa + AAbaB` is a chain.

This is worth being strict about for a reason that is particular to a shared searchable
record rather than to a paper: search here is literal text matching. If half the project
writes `A` and half writes `a^{-1}`, the two halves stop finding each other's records,
and the failure is silent -- a search returns "nothing matched", which reads as "nobody
has tried this".

### What a chain is

scl is not defined on an arbitrary group element. It is defined on the commutator
subgroup, and more generally on chains: formal sums of cyclically reduced conjugacy
classes whose total homology class is trivial.

In the free group F_2 = <a,b> this means a word must have equal numbers of a and A, and
equal numbers of b and B, before scl(w) means anything at all. For a word with nonzero
exponent sum, scl is undefined, or infinity if you prefer.

Note what the example above shows. The individual terms need not have trivial homology
class: `a` has exponent sum +1 in `a`, and `AAbaB` has exponent sum -1 in `a`. It is only
the total that vanishes. A chain is therefore not merely a formal sum of elements that
are each already in the commutator subgroup, and treating it as one is a mistake worth
naming.

Chains are also the right generality to work in, and not merely the largest domain on
which the definition makes sense. The arguments that compute scl -- cutting along a curve,
decomposing into arcs, gluing surfaces with corners -- naturally take chains as input and
produce chains as output, so a statement about single elements would have to be widened
to chains at the first step anyway. Pose questions about chains from the start.

Recorded because the commutator-subgroup point is the first thing a newcomer gets wrong,
and because a claim about the scl of an element outside the commutator subgroup is not
false but meaningless, which is harder to notice.
